lead: A VANET (vehicular ad hoc network) is a wireless network of moving vehicles. Links form as cars meet each other; roadside units (RSUs) beside the road are optional fixed access points, and the network still works without them. Road-constrained motion lets position and maps replace stable links. Safety warnings, tolling and traffic updates use it. Only a few universities teach this in depth. This chapter covers domains, applications and routing; the radio is in 6.8.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the in-vehicle bus, 6.6 for V2X (vehicle-to-everything) messages, and basic IP routing.

sections.h3: Ad hoc links and VANET domains

blocks.text: An ad hoc wireless network has no fixed infrastructure. Every node forwards packets for others, so distant nodes communicate in multiple hops. In a VANET each vehicle carries an on-board unit (OBU): a radio plus computer that sends and receives messages. A roadside unit (RSU) is a fixed access point beside the road. Multi-hop matters when an RSU is out of range: a warning can pass car to car until it reaches a highway patrol or a connected ambulance.

Three domains fit together. The in-vehicle domain is the electronic control unit (ECU) network on the car's buses (see 6.1). The OBU joins it to the ad hoc domain, where OBUs talk to OBUs and RSUs. RSUs connect to the infrastructure domain: Internet and cloud servers. Safety messages need the ad hoc path; a toll server can use infrastructure. The same OBU can also use cellular data, but ad hoc links work without a tower and add low delay locally.

Road traffic deaths exceed one million a year worldwide; most occur in low- and middle-income countries. VANET safety applications aim at this: collision warning ahead, hazard warning after a crash, and intersection warning at blind corners. Connected autonomous vehicles also need V2X because cameras and radar cannot see through buildings. Non-safety uses include traffic information, electronic tolling (FASTag in India), parking payment and infotainment. Safety messages are short and repeated; non-safety messages can tolerate delay.

The radio design differs from generic mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). Vehicles move at high speed, so a 200 m link between cars closing at 240 km/h lasts about 3 s. Contacts are short, yet paths are predictable because cars follow roads; the Global Positioning System (GPS) gives position. Vehicles have no energy limit, and the network can be very large. The message rate rises in dense traffic, so channel load is a design limit. These facts drive position-based routing.

sections.h3: Routing families and their failure modes

blocks.text: Topology-based routing stores routes to addresses. AODV (ad hoc on-demand distance vector) floods a route request, learns a route, and repairs broken links; DSR (dynamic source routing) carries the whole route in each packet. At highway speed links break before repair finishes. Routing chooses the next radio hop, not the whole road trip.

Position-based routing uses GPS coordinates. Greedy perimeter stateless routing (GPSR) first uses greedy forwarding: send to the neighbour closest to the destination. At a local maximum no neighbour is closer, so perimeter mode forwards the packet around the void by face routing on a planarized graph of the radio neighbours, using positions taken from GPS. The faces come from where the neighbours are, not from the road layout. The worked example applies the greedy rule.

Geocast sends a message to all vehicles in a target region, useful for a hazard zone. Simple flooding causes the broadcast storm problem: many vehicles rebroadcast the same alert and congest the channel. Suppression, such as waiting a random time or selecting one forwarder, reduces this. Where no next vehicle exists, store-and-forward carries the packet until a car or RSU appears.

examples.question: A packet at (0,0) must reach a destination at (100,0). Neighbours are A at (40,10), B at (70,−20) and C at (20,30). Which neighbour does greedy forwarding choose?
steps: For each neighbour compute distance to the destination with d = √((100−x)² + (0−y)²), where (x,y) is the neighbour position in metres.
The smallest distance is for B, about 36.1 m, so greedy forwarding sends to B.
examples.answer: Greedy forwarding sends the packet to neighbour B, about 36.1 m from the destination.

traps: VANET nodes are not energy-limited and move on roads; generic MANET assumptions such as random motion and battery limits fail.
AODV link repair cannot keep up with 120 km/h traffic, so 'topology routing always works' is false.
Greedy forwarding can stop at a local maximum; perimeter mode then recovers, and delivery is guaranteed only if the neighbour graph is connected and planarized, as GPSR assumes.
Flooding a hazard alert is not free: it causes the broadcast storm problem.
GPSR sends to the neighbour closest to the destination, not closest to the source; a common exam slip.

quiz.a: OBU: on-board unit in a vehicle; RSU: fixed roadside unit.

quiz.q: Name two safety and two non-safety VANET applications.
quiz.a: Safety: collision warning, hazard warning. Non-safety: tolling, infotainment.

quiz.q: Why is road-constrained motion useful for routing?
quiz.a: Vehicle paths are predictable and GPS gives position, so a packet can be forwarded toward a map position instead of a stored route.

quiz.q: A neighbour is at (60,80) and the destination at (100,0). Compute its distance to the destination.
Why can AODV fail at 120 km/h?
quiz.a: A link can break before route repair completes; new route discovery adds delay and overhead, so packets drop.

quiz.q: How does store-and-forward help on a sparse highway?
quiz.a: A vehicle keeps the packet and forwards when another vehicle or RSU enters range, bridging a gap that has no end-to-end path now.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is testing cellular V2X (C-V2X) alongside IEEE 802.11p, and RSUs increasingly run edge computing for local warnings. Search 'ETSI ITS-G5', 'C-V2X sidelink' and 'SUMO VANET simulation' for standards and mobility models. Security and privacy of beacon messages remain active research.
